passage: Parul, you think nobody at your office will understand. Let me tell you about the year I turned twenty-five. I'd pushed my bosses for months to try my new billing system at the mill. Big talk, I had. The first week it crashed, and the salaries went out three days late. Nobody shouted. That was worse. Everyone was so polite. "Bad luck, Harish-ji." "Happens to everyone." But I saw two colleagues by the tea urn, smiling at each other when I walked in and stopping when I came near. I ate lunch alone at my desk for a month. I felt the size of a pin. Then the old accounts clerk sat with me one day and said, "Let's find the bug." That's all. The system worked by winter. But I still remember those smiles, beta.

qa.q: How late did the salaries go out?
qa.a: Three days late.

qa.q: How did Harish feel in the month after the crash, and what shows it?
qa.a: Lonely and small, "the size of a pin". Harish ate lunch alone for a month, aware of colleagues smiling behind their polite words.

qa.q: What did the old accounts clerk do, and why did it matter so much?
qa.a: The clerk sat with Harish and said "Let's find the bug", offering real help instead of polite lines, which ended the isolation and led to the fix.

qa.q: What might hearing this be like for Parul, who feels nobody understands?
qa.a: Parul may feel less alone, hearing that Harish once felt "the size of a pin" too, and may take heart that one person's real help changed things.

grounding: An elder recalls how, at twenty-five, a failed project left them sensing colleagues' smiles behind polite words and feeling small and alone.

passage: The app launch Pankaj had led had flopped: barely two hundred downloads in a month. Now he had to explain it at the Monday review, and the office generator had failed, so there was no projector, just a hot room and his printouts. "So sorry about the numbers, Pankaj," said Uma, whose own plan had been turned down for his. Her voice was kind. The corner of her mouth wasn't. Across the table, two others exchanged a look he'd seen before, in the canteen, when someone's bike got towed. Pankaj's throat went dry. He read his pages to the table while sweat ran down his back, and he felt about eight years old. After the meeting, nobody walked out with him. He sat alone in the stairwell with his printouts, lonelier than at any time since he had joined.

qa.q: How many downloads did the launch get in a month?
qa.a: Barely two hundred.

qa.q: What did Pankaj suspect Uma was really feeling behind "So sorry about the numbers"?
qa.a: That Uma was secretly pleased, since her own plan had been turned down for his and the corner of her mouth didn't match her kind voice.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do after the stairwell so he isn't alone with the failure?
qa.a: Reach out to one trusted colleague or friend to talk it through, and focus the review on what can be learned rather than on the smiles.

qa.q: What would change if even one colleague had walked out with Pankaj?
qa.a: He might have felt less alone and small, and the others' smiles would have been easier to bear 🤍

passage: Chaitanya's design for a school library in Thane had been the office favourite, until the client rejected it in one line: "Too costly, not practical." By lunch, everyone at the Mumbai firm knew. People were polite. "Tough luck, yaar." "Their loss." But in the office chat group, someone posted a meme about "big dreams, small budgets", and three laughing faces appeared under it within a minute. Nobody named him. Nobody needed to. Chaitanya kept his eyes on his screen, drawing lines he would erase later. He felt see-through, and very small. At six, Lalit from the next desk set a cutting chai beside his keyboard. "The reading nook in your design is the best thing I've seen this year," Lalit said. "Budget can be fixed. Ideas like that can't." Chaitanya didn't answer right away. His eyes stung.

qa.q: What line did the client use to reject the design?
qa.a: "Too costly, not practical."

qa.q: How did the laughing faces under the meme make Chaitanya feel?
qa.a: See-through and very small, knowing colleagues were enjoying his failure even though nobody named him.

qa.q: What made Lalit's gesture helpful at that moment?
qa.a: Lalit brought chai and specific praise for the reading nook, separating the good idea from the budget problem, instead of polite lines or jokes.

qa.q: What might the colleagues who posted laughing faces not realise?
qa.a: They may think it was harmless fun, not realising Chaitanya could see it and felt lonely and exposed.

grounding: A young architect whose design was rejected senses colleagues' amusement behind polite words and feels small, until one colleague offers real kindness.

My name is Madhav, and I want to write down what last June felt like, because I still feel it. I'd led our lab's grant proposal for eight months. I told everyone it would get funded. It didn't. The email came on a Tuesday, and by lunch the whole floor knew.
Nobody was rude. Shankar patted my shoulder. "Tough one, man. The committee's so random." But he was smiling as he said it, just a little, and then I heard him laugh in the corridor with two others, and the laughing stopped when I came round the corner.
That's the part that hurt. Not the rejection. The feeling that my failure was somebody's small good news. I ate lunch alone that week, not because anyone excluded me, but because I felt smaller than the table.

qa.q: How long had Madhav led the grant proposal?
qa.a: For eight months.

qa.q: What feeling hurt Madhav more than the rejection itself?
qa.a: The sense that his failure was somebody's small good news, which left him feeling alone and smaller than the table.

qa.q: What could help Madhav in a week like that?
qa.a: Reaching out to one trusted colleague or friend outside the corridor talk, so the loneliness doesn't grow in silence.

qa.q: How might Shankar see his own smile, if he thought about it?
qa.a: Shankar might not have realised how visible it was, and could feel uncomfortable knowing Madhav noticed.

grounding: An adult whose proposal failed senses colleagues enjoying it and feels lonely and small.

Indu, twenty-four, had talked the farmers of Pipri village into trying the new millet seed on four plots. She had shown charts at the panchayat, promised better yields.
The rains came late. The millet came up thin and yellow.
At the cooperative meeting, Sunaina, who had wanted the old seed, said politely, "Nobody can control rain." But she and two farmers exchanged a look, and one of them grinned at the floor.
Indu felt her face burn. She wrote in her notebook so she wouldn't have to look up.
Walking home past the plots, she heard laughter from the tea shop and was sure it was about her. Maybe it wasn't. It felt like it.
That night she sat on the roof alone. The stars were very bright, and she felt very small under them.

qa.q: How many plots did the farmers try the new millet seed on?
qa.a: Four plots.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling as she wrote in her notebook without looking up?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and small, sensing Sunaina and the farmers enjoying her failure behind polite words.

qa.q: What could Indu do in the days ahead?

qa.a: Sunaina may feel vindicated, since she wanted the old seed, and may not notice how much her look hurt Indu.

The app Oskar's team had built for the Oslo council was pulled after two days. Too many bugs. His name was on the launch email.
At the Monday meeting his manager said, "It's a learning experience." People nodded. Nobody looked at him.
Except Kaito. Kaito had argued for a different design back in May. Now Oskar caught him smiling as he stirred his coffee, a small, private smile.
Oskar felt it in his stomach. He knew it might mean nothing. But it felt like being watched while he fell.
He ate his sandwich outside by the fjord, alone. His phone buzzed with a joke from the team chat about "bug season". Three laughing faces.
He switched it off, looked at the grey water, and felt about ten centimetres tall.

qa.q: How long was the app live before it was pulled?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling after catching Kaito's smile?
qa.a: He felt stung and exposed, as if Kaito was enjoying his failure.

Dear Dolma ma'am,
I hope it's all right to write to you. You were my first mentor, and I don't know who else to tell. The product launch I led failed last week; the app crashed on the first day and the client cancelled. I expected to feel embarrassed. What I didn't expect was the other thing.

Could we speak this week?
Harsha

Ujjwal, you asked why I stopped going to the Sunday market. I'll tell you. I'm Jahnavi, and when my little cafe closed in March, I thought the hard part would be the money. It wasn't. It was the faces.
The shop owners on our lane had watched me open with balloons and a poster that said "Best coffee in Indore". When I shut, they said, "Oh, so sad," but I could see them smiling. One aunty told another, loud enough, "Big poster, small cafe." They laughed. I walked home feeling about two inches tall.
It's strange: losing the cafe hurt, but being enjoyed while I lost it hurt more. That's why I go to the other market now. Nobody there knows the poster.

passage: Trisha had forty minutes to pack up her stall before the building shut. The pop-up bakery she'd pitched to the whole co-working space had sold eleven cupcakes in two days. 'Maybe next time,' someone called. Trisha smiled and said, 'Maybe.' Her hands shook as she taped the boxes. It wasn't the eleven cupcakes. It was the grins. On the bus home, with the rain hammering the windows, she felt tiny and very alone. She texted her flatmate: 'Can you just be home tonight?'
